claims.text: The starting composite contains tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments within a copper matrix.
The W–Cu composite develops phase separation under service conditions.
The W–Cu composite develops interfacial voids under service conditions.
A nanoscale HEA interlayer is to be coated onto tungsten surfaces before consolidation.
HEA-containing materials have been used for interface engineering in a metal-matrix composite.
The proposed composite can be consolidated using powder-metallurgy or spark-plasma-sintering conditions.
Ar+, He+, and D+ irradiation exposures are representative of the intended W-based plasma-facing/Cu-based cooling service environment.
The HEA interlayer lowers W–Cu interfacial energy and thereby improves wetting.
The HEA interlayer promotes interdiffusion across the W–Cu interface.
Improved wetting and interdiffusion minimize interfacial void formation and limit phase separation during thermal and irradiation stress.
The complex, compositionally stabilized structure of an HEA coating enhances bonding between tungsten and copper.
Improved interfacial bonding suppresses the disparities that drive phase segregation and void formation during cyclic thermal loading and irradiation.
Maintaining a continuous, defect-reduced W–Cu interface increases effective thermal conductivity.
HEA-coated W–Cu composites will have less interfacial void content than identically processed uncoated composites after thermal and irradiation exposure.
HEA-coated W–Cu composites will exhibit less phase separation than identically processed uncoated composites after thermal and irradiation exposure.
HEA-coated W–Cu composites will retain higher effective thermal conductivity than identically processed uncoated composites under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically develop significant voiding and phase separation under high thermal and irradiation loads, degrading joint-region thermal conductivity.
The proposed processing boundary extends to approximately 1600 °C.
Performance outside the stated temperature and irradiation ranges is untested.
